# ADR-284: A Nikaia Library for Other Languages Is One C Artifact — a Target That Is Safe at Its Boundary, Entry Points That Answer With a Status, the Caller's Memory, and Every Other Host a Generated File Over It

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** October 3, 2026 (D30-D32: October 10, 2026)
**History:** the records this one replaces are archived in [`docs/history/adr`](../../history/adr/README.md); read them only for how the decision was reached
**Answers:** the question *whether a binary Nikaia library needs a
single-threaded and a thread-safe build*;
[#88](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/88) (a library C and
every C-speaking host can call),
[#108](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/108) (a struct by
value), [#109](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/109) (the
symbol prefix), [#110](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/110)
(cancel and stream), [#111](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/111)
(the WebAssembly library), [#112](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/112)
(bindings), and whether Node gets a native add-on
**Related:** [ADR-302](adr-302.md) (the other
direction: calling C — `extern` reserved with its construct, a view and an
opaque handle);
[ADR-184](adr-184.md) D1 (a view is spelled `ref X`);
[ADR-037](adr-037.md) D1, D2, D7 (the target decides what `std` offers;
`user_parallelism` bounds *your* code; the per-value count);
[ADR-312](adr-312.md) D6, D9 and D11 (no verdict reads the switch; no `Shared`
at a foreign call);
[ADR-119](adr-119.md) D4, D7 (an allocator the build names; settings baked at
build time — reused here);
[ADR-010](adr-010.md) D1 (an FFI value is `Untrusted`);
[ADR-023](adr-023.md) D6 and [ADR-292](adr-292.md) (raise site and
`secondary`); [ADR-297](adr-297.md) (the cleanup deadline);
[ADR-100](adr-100.md), [ADR-308](adr-308.md), [ADR-005](adr-005.md) D8 (the
ledger, its hash, `--locked`); [ADR-277](adr-277.md) (a function-typed
parameter); [ADR-152](adr-152.md) D2 (`Array[T, N]`, D15's array field);
[ADR-292](adr-292.md) D14 (cancellation inside the language); [ADR-288](adr-288.md) D11 (an entry is written and
reviewed, not copied from Rust); [ADR-290](adr-290.md) (`nikaia describe`, the other
generated file); Part III 15.1, 15.3, 17.2, Appendix A

## 1. Question

**What does a Nikaia library look like to a program written in another
language?** A C program, a Python module, a Node or browser page, a Java
service over Panama: every one of those hosts speaks the C calling convention,
and the comfortable bindings (`PyO3`, `napi-rs`) are wrappers over the same
entry points. So the C ABI is the floor every other host stands on, and the
question has six parts:

1. **Threads.** A library is called by somebody who owns the threads. Is that a
   third value of `user_parallelism`, a second artifact, or something else?
2. **The entry point.** How is one written, what crosses, in whose memory, how
   does a failure, a panic or a pause arrive at a caller with no executor, and
   how does the library start and stop in a process it does not own?
3. **Small aggregates.** A `Point { x, y }` as an opaque handle with `_new` and
   `_free` around two doubles is not what a C programmer expects.
4. **Names.** May a declaration choose its own symbol?
5. **Cancel and stream.** How does a host stop an asynchronous call, and how do
   many results cross?
6. **Other hosts.** Is the web a second calling convention, and is Python or
   Node a second artifact?

The question cannot wait for a program: the first target added without these
answers would answer them by accident.

## 2. How others do it

| Language / tool | Its answer | What it costs there |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| CPython C extensions | the GIL serialises callers | a C extension may release it around its own work, and free-threaded CPython removes it — one caller thread is not a promise |
| `PyO3`, `napi-rs` | a native module per host language | a second translation table (Python objects, JS values) beside the C one, a second build dependency, a second thing out of date |
| Rust | `#[repr(C)]` gives a struct C's layout | one attribute; a packed layout reads slowly and cannot be borrowed into |
| Rust and every web toolchain on `wasm32` | a module's exports are C-convention functions; the host reaches the module's memory only | no second convention; the host must take its buffers from the module |
| Well-aged C libraries | the caller owns the memory; a call returns a status, never unwinds, never blocks unannounced; names prefixed consistently | the caller passes buffers and checks every return |
| Java (Panama), C# (P/Invoke), Go (cgo) | load a C library with their own means | nothing the library has to do |

**What does not transfer:** a native module per language assumes the compiler
should own every host's object model; this compiler owns one ledger, and every
host-facing file is a projection of it.

## 3. Options, weighed

| Option | Rejected by | Why it lost |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A third value of `user_parallelism` for "foreign code calls in" | D1 | the switch bounds *your* code; asking it about a caller's threads makes it mean two things, the second silently |
| Two artifacts, single-threaded and thread-safe, the consumer picks | D2 | two of everything to build and name, and a wrong pick is a data race, not an error |
| The safe shape (atomic count, real lock) on every value | D2 | pays everywhere for a property only the boundary has — the cost ADR-037 D7 was built to stop |
| A NUL-terminated string scanned for, results allocated by the library | D5, D6 | the length is a fact the caller has; memory the caller did not ask for is what an embedded, garbage-collected or fuzzing host cannot take |
| Unwind into C, or abort | D8 | unwinding into C is undefined behaviour; aborting ends a process that is not ours |
| A handle for every exported struct | D14 | ten thousand samples become ten thousand handles |
| A per-declaration rename (`as "name"`, an attribute) | D13 | the header stops being a projection of the ledger, and a reader cannot find a function by its symbol |
| A queue behind a stream | D21 | a buffer grows behind the host's back; the callback's return is already the backpressure |
| Returning a `Vec` of text or handles, or a `Seq` | D20 | no shape for it in C; the refusal names the callback idiom instead |
| `extern "wasm"` | D22 | a second word for the same convention; what differs on the web is memory and thread, not the call |
| `set_allocator` and a blocking form on WebAssembly | D23, D24 | one linear memory the module already manages; the host's one thread must not block |
| `artifact = "python-module"`, a native module per language | D26 | a second artifact, a second table, a second dependency |
| A `napi` dependency in the emitted crate, or building a Node add-on now | D28 | a second artifact reopens *which artifact is the program*; nothing in the tree needs it |

## 4. Decision

The rules are grouped as the question is: the target (D1-D3), the entry point
(D4-D13), the value struct (D14-D18), cancel and stream (D19-D21), WebAssembly
(D22-D25), other hosts (D26-D29).

### D1 — Whether foreign code may call in is a property of the target, not a third value of `user_parallelism`.

The target already decides what `std` offers and what a panic does
([ADR-037](adr-037.md) D1) — *what is outside this program, and what it does to
us*. `user_parallelism` bounds **your** code and cannot answer for a caller's.
A build that exports entry points is therefore a target of its own: the pair
`target` + `artifact` (D4).

### D2 — One build, safe at its boundary: not two artifacts, not the safe shape everywhere.

Every exported entry point, and everything reachable from one, takes the safe
count and the safe lock; everything else keeps the per-value answer
([ADR-037](adr-037.md) D7). An entry point is a **root** seeded at the floor of
the analysis that already answers per value.

### D3 — The checks do not change, because no check reads the switch.

The crossing verdict is about a type and a destination
([ADR-312](adr-312.md) D6, [ADR-312](adr-312.md) D11), and a ledger contract is
written at the floor. A library with foreign entry points is already checked
for the world it enters; only what is **emitted** moves, under its entry points.
A C signature names neither count shape, so [ADR-312](adr-312.md) D9's
representation problem does not return; what returns is the ownership of
threads.

### D4 — `pub extern "C" fn` with a body is an entry point; `artifact = "c-library"` makes the library; `"C"` is the only string.

*Changed by [ADR-324](adr-324.md) D6: written `extern`, without `"C"`; `extern "C"` is `NK1227`.*

```nika
pub extern "C" fn greet(name: ref String) -> String { f"Hello, {name}" }
```

`extern "C"` before a body is [ADR-302](adr-302.md)'s word in its second form:
the block without a body declares a function the language calls; a function
with one is a function it provides. `artifact = "c-library"` in `[build]`,
beside `target`, makes a shared and a static library and `<package>.h`
generated from the ledger. Four refusals at the declaration: `extern` without
`pub`; a body in a build without a library artifact; a generic function or a
trait method; a signature D5 does not cover, naming the shape to use. The
string names the calling convention and is `"C"` on every target (D22).

### D5 — What crosses, and what it is in the header.

| in the declaration | in C | rule |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `i32`, `i64`, `u8`, `f64`, `bool`, `char` | `int32_t`, `int64_t`, `uint8_t`, `double`, `bool`, `uint32_t` | by value, both ways |
| `ref String`, `ref Array[u8]`, `Bytes` **in** | pointer and `size_t` | never a terminator; the caller keeps it; text not UTF-8 is a status |
| `String`, `Bytes`, `Vec[u8]` **out** | `uint8_t* out, size_t cap, size_t* written` | the caller's buffer (D6) |
| a list of numbers **in** | `const int64_t*`, `size_t` | an array the caller keeps |
| a `pub extern "C" struct` | the struct, by value | D14-D16 |
| any other exported `pub struct` | `struct <package>_<Type>*`, opaque | a handle: its `extern` constructor, `<package>_<Type>_free`, a getter per `pub` field, its `extern` methods |
| `enum` without payload | a C `enum` | numbered in declaration order; appended, never reordered |
| `enum` with payload | an opaque handle, `_kind` and a getter per field | as a struct (D31) |
| a `pub extern enum` | a tagged union, by value | D32 |
| `T?` of a handle or text | `NULL` | |
| `T?` of a number | the value's out-parameter and `bool* present` | C has no absent integer; the status stays `OK` (D30) |
| `fn(A) -> R sync` parameter | a function pointer and `void* ctx` | called on the calling thread, or a library thread for D9's async form; a pausing callback is refused; a `bool` return is the stream's stop (D20) |
| `Locked`, `Shared`, `Seen`, a map, a list of anything else | — | refused, naming a handle around a struct, or a callback for many results |

Every value that enters is `Untrusted` ([ADR-010](adr-010.md) D1).

### D6 — The caller owns the memory.

A text or bytes result is written into the caller's buffer: at most `cap`
bytes, `written` set to the full length, `E_TOO_SMALL` with `written` the size
that would do, `out == NULL` the size query. What the library holds across
calls comes from `<package>_set_allocator(alloc, free, ctx)` if the caller
calls it before `init`, the platform heap otherwise. What a callback receives
is a view that lives for the call. (On WebAssembly the host takes its buffers
from the module instead, D23.)

### D7 — Every entry point returns an `int` status, and a value travels in an out-parameter.

`0` is `<PACKAGE>_OK`; a `throws` function's variants are `1…`, per library in
declaration order, `<PACKAGE>_E_<VARIANT>`, part of the ABI. Seven negative
codes are the boundary's, the same in every library: `-1 E_ARGUMENT`,
`-2 E_TOO_SMALL`, `-3 E_NOT_RUNNING`, `-4 E_PANICKED`, `-5 E_REENTRANT`,
`-6 E_CLEANUP`, `-7 E_CANCELLED`. `<package>_last_error(out, cap, written)`
renders this thread's last failure with its raise site
([ADR-023](adr-023.md) D6) and `secondary` list ([ADR-292](adr-292.md)).

### D8 — A panic never leaves the library: it is caught at the boundary and poisons it.

The emitted crate of a library artifact **unwinds** — the one artifact where
Appendix A's abort at `user_parallelism = no` does not hold, because the host
survives. Every entry point catches, returns `E_PANICKED`, and every later call
does too until `shutdown` and `init` have run. The panic hook runs first.

### D9 — A function that may pause is exported blocking and `_async`.

`<package>_fetch(…)` blocks the calling thread, which drives that one future
itself over the shared reactor. `<package>_fetch_async(…, done, ctx, op)`
returns at once; `done(status, ctx)` runs on a library thread; `op` is D19's
ticket. A `sync` function has the blocking form only. On WebAssembly only the
async form exists (D24).

### D10 — The runtime starts on the first call or on `init`, and stops on `shutdown`.

`<package>_init()` is idempotent and safe from any thread; every entry point
calls it if nobody has. `<package>_shutdown()` drains cleanups within
`cleanup-deadline` and returns `E_CLEANUP`, naming the resources, where it
expires — never ending the process. After it, every call is `E_NOT_RUNNING`;
`set_allocator` after `init` is `E_ARGUMENT`. `nikaia-runtime.toml` is read at
build time and baked in, as [ADR-119](adr-119.md) D7 does; `user-pool` sizes
the library's executor.

### D11 — A handle carries a lock, and a re-entrant call on it is a status.

Exclusive for a method the ledger marks `mutates`, shared otherwise, held for
the call. A call from the thread already holding it, on the same handle, is
`E_REENTRANT` instead of a deadlock.

### D12 — The header is generated from the ledger and carries its hash; `--locked` catches an ABI change.

`<package>.h` is derived from `nikaia.contracts` and carries its hash and the
package version; a changed exported signature changes the ledger, and a
`--locked` build refuses until it is committed ([ADR-100](adr-100.md),
[ADR-308](adr-308.md)).

### D13 — The compiler names every symbol: one prefix, and no declaration renames itself.

`<prefix>_<fn>`, `<prefix>_<Type>_<method>`, `<prefix>_<Type>_new` for the
anonymous constructor, `_free`, `<prefix>_<Type>_<field>`; constants
`<PREFIX>_OK`, `<PREFIX>_E_<VARIANT>`, `<PREFIX>_<TYPE>_<VARIANT>`. The prefix
is the package name with `-` written `_`, or the one `symbol-prefix` in
`[build]`; it is a C identifier or the build refuses it, naming the character.
There is no `as "name"` and no attribute: what a program wants called
differently outside, it renames inside. A collision after prefixing is refused
at the declaration; only these symbols are visible in the artifact.

### D14 — `pub extern "C" struct` has C's layout and crosses by value.

```nika
pub extern "C" struct Point { pub x: f64, pub y: f64 }
```

Fields in declaration order with C's alignment and padding (`#[repr(C)]`
below), written into the header as a `typedef struct`. In, out, as a parameter,
a result and a field, by value; no handle, `_new`, `_free`, getter or lock.
Inside the language it is an ordinary struct.

### D15 — A field is a C value, and every field is `pub`.

A number, `bool`, `char`, a payload-free `enum`, another `extern "C"` struct,
or an `Array[T, N]` of one of these ([ADR-152](adr-152.md) D2: inline, laid out
as C lays it out). Anything else — text, bytes, a list, an optional, a lock, a
`Shared`, a function, a struct without the word — is `NK1145`, whose message
names the handle as the shape to use.

### D16 — Its rows in the table, and its methods.

In or out: by value. A `Vec` of them **in**: `const <prefix>_T*`, `size_t`.
**Out**: the caller's buffer counted in elements, with D6's size query and
`E_TOO_SMALL`. `T?` of one: `bool* present`, as for a number (D30). A
method is `<prefix>_<Type>_<method>` with `self` as `const T*`, or `T*` where it
changes it — and **no lock**: a value struct is the caller's memory and two
threads writing one is the caller's race, which the header says.

### D17 — The layout is part of the ABI, and the ledger carries it.

Field order and types are in `nikaia.contracts`; a reordered, retyped or
appended field changes the hash and `--locked` refuses. There is no versioning
in the struct: a library that must stay binary-compatible across an added
field exports a handle.

### D18 — The same type serves the other direction.

An `extern "C"` struct is also what a declared C function of
[ADR-302](adr-302.md)'s block takes or returns by value. One word, one layout,
both directions; a value struct carries no address.

### D19 — The `_async` form takes an optional ticket, and `<prefix>_cancel` cancels at the next pause point.

`<prefix>_op** op` is the last parameter; `NULL` allocates nothing.
`<prefix>_cancel(op)` cancels the task at its next pause point, as a `select`
loser is, with its `cleanup` run under `cleanup-deadline`. `done` is called
**exactly once**: the work's status, or `E_CANCELLED` when cancellation came
first. Cancel after `done`, or twice, is `OK`. The caller frees the ticket with
`<prefix>_op_free` after `done`; before it, that is `E_ARGUMENT` and the ticket
is kept. The blocking form has no cancellation.

### D20 — A stream is a function that takes a callback, and the callback's `bool` is the caller's stop.

```nika
pub extern "C" fn lines(path: ref String, each: fn(ref String) -> bool sync) throws { … }
```

`each` is called once per item, the item a view for the call; `false` ends the
function with `OK`. A callback returning nothing streams without a stop. A
function that returns a `Vec` of text, a `Vec` of handles or a `Seq` is
refused with *write it as a function that takes `fn(item) -> bool sync`*.

### D21 — Backpressure is the callback's return, not a queue.

The next item is produced after the callback returns, never before: at most one
item in flight per call. A host that wants a queue builds it in memory it owns.

### D22 — A WebAssembly library is the same entry point on another target.

`target = "wasm32-unknown"` with `artifact = "c-library"` makes `<package>.wasm`,
`<package>.js` (an ES module for browser and Node) and `<package>.d.ts` from the
same declarations and ledger; the `.js` is the header for a host without
headers. `extern "wasm"` is refused: *the convention is `"C"` on every target;
the target names WebAssembly*. Everything of D4-D13 holds except where memory
and thread differ (D23, D24).

### D23 — The host obtains its buffers from the module.

`<prefix>_alloc(size, align) -> i32` and `<prefix>_free(ptr, size, align)`;
the `.js` does the asking, writing, reading and freeing, so a caller writes
`hello.render("name")`. No `set_allocator`. A handle is an offset wrapped in a
class with `free()`, registered with `FinalizationRegistry` where offered — a
convenience, not a guarantee.

### D24 — A pausing entry point has only the callback form, and the `.js` makes it a Promise.

No blocking form. The module's executor is driven from the host's event loop;
each pausing function is a `Promise`, cancellable through an `AbortSignal` that
maps to `<prefix>_cancel`. A `sync` entry point is called plainly.

### D25 — What a WebAssembly library may do is what its target's `std` offers.

Part III 17.2's availability table decides; the host's `fetch`, timers and
storage reach the module through the mechanism the target already uses for its
I/O worker. Entry points change nothing about it.

### D26 — `nikaia bind <language>` writes a binding over the C library; the artifact stays one.

`nikaia bind python` writes `<package>/__init__.py` over `ctypes`; `nikaia bind
js` is D22's `.js` and `.d.ts`. A binding is generated source the host loads
with what it ships, regenerated with the header, carrying the same ledger hash.
There is no `artifact = "python-module"`.

### D27 — What the Python binding makes of the boundary.

A non-`OK` status is an exception (`<pkg>.Error` with a subclass per variant,
`<pkg>.BoundaryError` subclasses for the negative codes, carrying
`last_error`); buffers are `str` or `bytes` with the size query done for the
caller; a handle is a class with methods, properties, `close()`, a context
manager and `__del__`; a value struct is a `ctypes.Structure`; an `enum` an
`IntEnum`; `T?` is `None`; a callback a callable kept alive by `CFUNCTYPE`;
`_async` a callable form and, under a running loop, an awaitable through
`call_soon_threadsafe` whose `cancel()` is the ticket; a stream a generator.
The wrapper locks only around `init` and `shutdown`.

### D28 — JavaScript is served by the WebAssembly build; a native Node add-on, where Node must reach a file or a socket, is generated C.

For JavaScript the binding is the WebAssembly build, which runs in a browser
and in Node without a native compile. Where a program needs Node to reach a file or
a socket, which the WebAssembly build cannot, `nikaia bind node` writes an N-API
shim **in C** over the C library, which the host's toolchain compiles — and
never a `napi` dependency in the emitted crate, which would be a second
artifact.

### D29 — A binding never widens what the library exports.

Only the entry points: no function the ledger does not mark `extern`, no field
the header does not read, no constructor the library lacks. What a host cannot
express is decided in the binding's table, not per program.

### D30 — An absent value is a flag beside it, not a status.

*Changes D5 and D16, which named a status `<PACKAGE>_NONE` and gave it no value.*

A `T?` of a number, or of an `extern` struct, comes out through two
out-parameters: the value's, and `bool* present` after it. The status is `OK`
whether the value is there or not; where `present` is `false` the value's
out-parameter is left untouched.

```c
int64_t n; bool present;
int s = lib_find(key, len, &n, &present);   /* s == LIB_OK; present says whether n holds */
```

A status keeps one meaning: `0` is a call that worked, anything else one that
did not. A binding makes the pair its language's absent value: `None` in
Python (D27), `null` in Node (D28).

**Rejected:** a status for the absent value, either as an eighth negative code
(`-8`), where a caller's `if (s < 0)` treats an ordinary *not found* as the
boundary failing, or as `1` with the variants from `2`, where it sits among the
errors and renumbers them. A positive code that is no error is what makes
SQLite's `SQLITE_ROW` and `SQLITE_DONE` easy to mistake.

### D31 — A handle to an `enum` with payload is read through `_kind` and a getter per field of each variant.

`<prefix>_<Type>_kind(h, &kind)` writes the variant as a C `enum`
(`<PREFIX>_<TYPE>_<VARIANT>`). A field's getter is
`<prefix>_<Type>_<Variant>_<field>`; a field without a name is numbered from
`0` in its variant, as Rust's `.0`, so `Circle(f64)` is read by
`<prefix>_Shape_Circle_0`. A getter called on a handle that holds another
variant returns `E_ARGUMENT` and leaves its out-parameter untouched;
`last_error` names the variant the handle holds.

**Rejected:** a boundary code of its own for the wrong variant, which every
library and binding would carry for a case `_kind` already answers; and a
panic, which would poison a library that did nothing wrong.

### D32 — `pub extern enum` is a tagged union and crosses by value.

```nika
pub extern enum Shape { Circle(f64), Rect { w: f64, h: f64 }, Empty }
```

As `pub extern struct` is to a struct (D14), so `pub extern enum` is to an
`enum` with payload: C's layout, no handle. The header writes it as
`#[repr(C)]` lays it out, which is what `cbindgen` writes for such an enum:

```c
typedef enum { LIB_SHAPE_CIRCLE, LIB_SHAPE_RECT, LIB_SHAPE_EMPTY } lib_Shape_Tag;
typedef struct {
    lib_Shape_Tag tag;
    union {
        struct { double _0; } circle;
        struct { double w; double h; } rect;
    };
} lib_Shape;
```

* A variant's fields follow D15: each a C value, an `extern enum` among them,
  anything else `NK1145`. A variant without fields has no member in the union.
  A field without a name is `_0`, `_1`, …; a variant's member is its name in
  lower case.
* It crosses as D16 says for an `extern` struct: in and out by value, a `Vec`
  as an array in and the caller's buffer out, its methods with `self` as
  `const T*` or `T*`, no lock. It is a C value itself, so it may be the field
  of an `extern` struct or of another `extern enum`.
* On the way in, a `tag` that names no variant is `E_ARGUMENT`, and the
  variant's fields are checked as D15's are.
* Its layout is ABI, carried by the ledger, as D17 says: a variant reordered,
  retyped or appended changes the hash.
* Inside the language it is an ordinary `enum`.
* A binding makes it its language's form: a `ctypes.Structure` with the union
  in Python (D27), an object `{ kind: "Rect", w, h }` in Node (D28).

## 5. Consequences

* **A Nikaia library ships once.** It is callable from anything that speaks C,
  safe at its boundary and per-value inside; the header, the `.js` and the
  Python file need no author and carry the ledger's hash.
* **The caller decides where memory lives**, and nothing that leaves the
  library can dangle: results are copied into the caller's buffer, handles are
  freed through the library, callback views end with the call.
* **A failure is a status the caller cannot miss**, a panic is one too, and a
  poisoned library says so rather than limping.
* **The program inside is ordinary Nikaia.** The C shapes are the emitter's.
* **What it costs:** the artifact key and `symbol-prefix`; the safe shape
  seeded at entry points; the emitter's wrappers (status, out-parameters,
  buffer protocol, allocator forwarder, catch at the boundary, blocking and
  async forms, ticket, handle lock); `#[repr(C)]` and `NK1145`; the header,
  `.js`/`.d.ts` and Python generators; baked settings; the executor bridge to a
  host's event loop.
* **Order:** after `std::db`, before the bare-metal target
  ([ADR-119](adr-119.md)), which reuses the allocator and baked settings.

## 6. What this does not decide

* **An exported `Locked[T]`**, and the bridge type of [ADR-312](adr-312.md) D9.
* **A fixed-size array, union, bit-field or packed layout** beyond D15's
  `Array[T, N]`: no counterpart, or a protocol that parses bytes.
* **A versioned symbol, and a linker symbol map**.
* **A library-side timeout, progress reporting, a cancellable blocking call**.
  Cancellation from user code inside the language is
  [ADR-292](adr-292.md) D14's.
* **The component model and WIT; threads on the web**.
* **Java, C# and Go generators; packaging as a wheel or an npm package; which
  hosts get a binding at all; WASI for the WebAssembly build's file access**.
* **Calling C from the language** — [ADR-302](adr-302.md), the other
  direction.
